lesson.title: Geometry: Properties, Congruence and Similarity
lesson.summary: This lesson explores how to use geometric properties, angle relationships, congruence, similarity and circle theorems to justify conclusions and solve problems.

objectives.text: Use geometric properties, angle relationships, congruence, similarity and circle theorems to solve problems.

sections.heading: Angle Relationships and Shape Properties
sections.body: Geometry becomes safer when each result has a named reason. Angles on a straight line total 180°, angles around a point total 360°, and vertically opposite angles are equal. In parallel lines, corresponding and alternate angles are equal while co-interior angles sum to 180°. A triangle has interior angles totalling 180°, so if two angles are 48° and 67°, the third is 65°. Write the relationship before subtracting. Do not measure a drawing that is not stated to scale. Use a quick sketch to mark the known angle, identify the relationship, and then check whether the answer is acute, obtuse, or a plausible triangle angle.

sections.heading: Congruence and Similarity
sections.body: Congruent shapes have exactly the same size and shape, even if one is rotated or reflected. Valid congruence tests include SSS, SAS, ASA, and RHS for right-angled triangles; matching only two angles proves similarity, not congruence. Similar shapes have equal corresponding angles and a constant scale factor between corresponding lengths. If a small triangle has sides 3, 4, and 5 and a similar triangle has scale factor 2.5, its sides are 7.5, 10, and 12.5. Areas scale by the square of the length factor, so the area factor is 6.25. Match corresponding vertices consistently, write the scale factor as new ÷ original, and use it in the correct direction.

sections.heading: Circle Theorems
sections.body: Circle theorems connect angles, chords, and tangents. The angle at the centre is twice the angle at the circumference standing on the same arc. Angles in the same segment are equal, and the angle in a semicircle is 90°. A tangent is perpendicular to the radius at the point of contact; the two tangents from an external point have equal lengths. When solving, identify the arc or chord first, state the theorem, and then calculate. If the central angle is 112°, the matching circumference angle is 56°. Use the diagram only to identify the stated relationships, not to estimate sizes. A final check is that angles in a triangle or around a point still satisfy the basic totals.

writingActivity.title: Justify a geometric conclusion
writingActivity.prompt: Choose an angle, similarity, or circle-theorem example. Write a short proof with one reason per line, then explain how you checked that the result fits the shape.
checklist: I named the theorem or congruence test.
I matched corresponding sides or angles consistently.
I checked the final result against a basic angle or scale fact.

practice.prompt: A triangle has angles of 50 degrees and 60 degrees. What is the third angle?
practice.explanation: The sum of angles in a triangle is 180 degrees, so 180 minus 50 and 60 equals 70.

practice.prompt: Two triangles have all corresponding angles equal and sides in a 1:2 ratio. Are they congruent or similar?
practice.explanation: Equal angles and proportional sides define similarity, not congruence, which requires equal side lengths.

practice.prompt: An angle at the centre of a circle is 100 degrees. What is the angle at the circumference on the same arc?
practice.explanation: The angle at the circumference is half the angle at the centre, so 100 divided by 2 is 50.
